newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - NZ grower tries to upset apple-cart.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - NZ grower tries to upset apple-cart.

text.p: A New Zealand apple grower is trying to overturn a marketing board's export monopoly in a challenge to established practice that could herald dramatic change in the country's crucial agricultural sector.
Producer boards were established by legislation after World War Two to ensure New Zealand companies did not undercut each other's prices and to give sellers more clout on world markets.
But many commentators believe their day is past in the mostly deregulated and open New Zealand economy.
The country's biggest apple exporter, South Island-based Apple Fields, threatened two weeks ago to rip out all its trees if its latest licence application fails to break the monopoly.
RULING EXPECTED
The application is currently being heard by the Apple and Pear Marketing Board (NZAPMB) -- the very body Apple Fields is challenging -- and the company expects a ruling early next week.

Legislation gives the board the power to control apple and pear exports. It has in the past allowed Apple Fields to export independently up to 59,000 cartons of apples but the company has applied to export its entire crop of around 1.5 million cartons.

Apple Fields, which represents six percent of the national crop with nearly 700 hectares in pipfruit (apples and pears), has campaigned for years against the NZAPMB's protected status as the country's prime pipfruit exporter, citing poor grower returns as reason enough for change.
Apple Fields general manager of commercial operations, Tom Suckling, said if the board refuses the export licence it will expose itself to a lot of criticism.
"They'll be seen to drive the biggest grower in New Zealand out of the apple business," he told Reuters.
But NZAPMB chairman John McCliskie said production was increasing in many areas of New Zealand and the hole left by the loss of Apple Fields' input would soon be filled.
"At the end of the day we just have to keep reminding people I represent 1,600 growers of which Apple Fields are one, and I have to try to act in the interests of the majority," he said.
Most of New Zealand's apple growers support the board's monopoly, and industry experts suggest Apple Fields is unlikely to get its licence.
They say the latest challenge has raised critical issues, not least the future of New Zealand's other two producer boards with export monopolies, if consent is granted.
OTHERS WATCHING
The Kiwifruit Marketing Board (NZKMB) and the Dairy Board (NZDB) are keeping close tabs on the situation.
It is possible that Apple Fields' challenge could change public and political attitudes toward statutory monopolies.

The NZDB is the largest multinational dairy marketing organisation in the world with annual exports of NZ$6 billion. Its group manager of public affairs, Neville Martin, said while theoretically the dairy industry could suffer from the splintering seen in the pipfruit industry, it was unlikely.
The board gave dairy companies the critical mass to tackle the world's big players head on, and enjoyed strong support.

"If the licence were granted to Apple Fields that obviously would be a precedent, but one which would not logically tip over to another industry unless you had a dairy company which wished to break from the pack and go its own way," he told Reuters.
"There isn't that ambition amongst the dairy companies in New Zealand... They fortunately can see a little further than the next dollar," Martin said.
Kiwifruit growers are not as cohesive as dairy farmers in backing their board, and several of the board's marketing strategies have come under fire.
NZ Business Roundtable executive director Roger Kerr said world trends in the fruit industry are for deregulation and the days of single-desk exporters are numbered, even in dairying.

"There is growing recognition that there should be alternatives. As time goes on, the producer board structures are standing out more and more as an anomaly in the New Zealand commercial environment," Kerr said.
He pointed out that the NZAPMB was obliged to consider independents' export applications after a 1993 law change, partly attributed to Apple Fields' lobbying.

If Apple Fields' latest application is declined, Kerr said, the members of parliament who in 1993 thought they were opening up a viable opportunity for independent exporting will conclude the legislation is not working.
"Nobody would then appear to be meeting any criteria that the board chooses to apply, and that would seem to be contrary to parliament's expectations at the time," Kerr said.
"One way or another I think those things are going to become issues for the new parliament in the not too distant future."
New Zealand's main political parties are currently negotiating to form a coalition after October's election.
DOUBTS ABOUT DAIRY BOARD

Federated Farmers president Malcolm Bailey said that in the dairy industry, a rash of mergers in the last six months and the increasing strength of key companies had cast some doubts over the viability of the Dairy Board.
Bailey said some people felt that if the number of big dairy companies fell to two or three, those companies would not accept a single seller system.
"I think the industry has to continue to prepare itself to operate without that statutory backing," Bailey said.

The Dairy Board's Martin agreed it was possible that rationalisation could spell the end of the board's monopoly if that was what dairy companies wanted. But while it remained advantageous to present a united international front, the present structure would continue.

Agricultural exports are the mainstay of New Zealand's export economy. Meat, wool and dairy products accounted for 33 percent of its total exports last year, while fruit and nuts were another 4.2 percent. (NZ$1 = US$0.71)
